transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. I... well, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten so far off track lately. Mostly, I just don't feel like myself anymore, you know? It's like the engine is running but the transmission is completely shot. I used to be the kind of guy who was always doing something, always on the move, especially with my line of work. But lately... I've just completely stopped doing everything that used to make me, well, me. 

I stopped hiking, which is huge because I used to be out on the trails every single weekend, rain or shine, logging miles and clearing my head. And coaching—I used to coach, and I just walked away from it. I don't even pick up my guitar anymore. It's just sitting there in its stand in the corner of the room collecting dust, and I look at it, and I just feel... nothing. No drive to play a single chord. I'm not even calling people back. My phone will ring, or I'll get a message, and I just stare at the screen. I know I should answer, I know they're probably wondering what's going on with me, but I just can't bring myself to hit the button and talk. 

It's gotten to the point where some days, honestly, I just sit in that small rental of mine for hours. Just sitting there in a chair. I'll look at the mess, or think about how I need to get up and take care of basic things, knowing perfectly well there are things to do, things I absolutely have to do... but I can't make myself start. I just sit there and watch the hours go by, and I can't force myself to move. It's just... it's really not how I used to be.
Have you ever experienced periods in your life where you felt unusually energetic, talkative, or productive, to the point where you felt like you didn't need much sleep?

No... no, I can't say I've ever had anything like that. I mean, sure, back when I was younger, working the night shift, sometimes I'd get off work and be a little wired, you know? Just from the adrenaline of the job, dealing with whatever calls came in. You get off at 6 AM, and the sun is coming up, and you think, 'Well, I should sleep,' but your body is still humming from the shift. But even then, I'd eventually crash. I'd go home, pull the blackout curtains shut, and sleep for a solid seven or eight hours. 

I've never had a time where I just didn't need sleep. Sleep has always been pretty important to me, actually. I used to be really strict about my schedule, making sure I got enough rest so I could be sharp on the job. You have to be sharp, you know? You can't be out there half-asleep when people are depending on you to keep them safe. So, no, I've never had a period where I was just bouncing off the walls, talking a mile a minute, or feeling like I could run on two hours of sleep. 

Honestly, it's always been the opposite, especially lately. It's just this heavy, dragging feeling. Like I said, I just sit there. I'm not energized at all. I'm just... drained. Completely drained, even when I haven't done anything all day. So, no, nothing like what you're describing. Never.
Have you ever felt this way for a period of two weeks or more at any other time in your life, perhaps years ago?

No, no, nothing like this. I mean, sure, everyone has a bad day, or maybe even a bad week, you know? Like back in '08, when the economy tanked, I was pretty stressed out for a while. We were getting a lot of calls at work, tensions were high everywhere, people were losing their homes... it was a rough patch for everyone. I remember feeling really down for a few days, just thinking about how messed up everything was, how hard people were struggling. But that was just stress, you know? It was situational. I still got up, put on the uniform, went to work, did my job. I still went hiking on my days off to blow off steam. 

I never, ever felt like this. This is entirely different. It's not just a bad mood or feeling stressed about something specific. It's like... it's like a switch flipped and the power got cut to the whole building, and it's been off for weeks now. I've never had a time where I just couldn't make myself move, where I couldn't care about anything for weeks on end. Even when my dad passed away, which was, God, that was awful... I grieved, obviously, I was sad, I cried. But I didn't just shut down completely and stare at the wall for weeks. I still had to take care of his estate, plan the funeral, call the relatives. I functioned. 

So, no, to answer your question, I've never had a two-week period, or even a one-week period, where I felt like this. This heavy, empty, paralyzed feeling... this is completely new. And it's terrifying, honestly. Because I don't know how to fix it. I'm used to fixing things, managing situations, taking control. And right now, I have absolutely zero control over my own body and mind. It's just... it's never happened before. Never.
When you are sitting there feeling this way, have you had any thoughts that life is not worth living or that you would be better off if you were no longer here?

No... no, I haven't. I mean, I know why you're asking, because it sounds like I'm just sitting there rotting away, and I guess in a way I am, but... no. I don't want to die. I don't sit there thinking about ending it or anything like that. It's not that I want to be gone, it's just that I don't know how to *be* here right now, if that makes sense. 

I'll sit in that chair, and I'll look out the window, and I'll see people walking their dogs or driving by, going about their lives, and I don't think, 'I wish I was dead.' I think, 'How are they doing that? How are they just... moving?' Because for me, the connection between wanting to do something and actually doing it is just severed. But it's not a death wish. 

Even on the worst days, when the apartment is a wreck and I haven't showered and I'm just staring at the dust motes in the air for hours... I don't think about hurting myself. I've seen enough of that in my line of work, believe me. You go on calls where someone decided they couldn't take it anymore, and you see the aftermath. You see the families. You see what it does to the people left behind. I've had to be the one to break the news, or stand there while the paramedics do what they can, knowing it's too late. It's an ugly, terrible thing, and I've seen it up close too many times. 

So no, I don't want that. I don't want to check out. I just want... I want the engine to turn over again. I want to feel like I can stand up and walk out the door and actually care about what happens next. I want to be the guy who gets up at 5 AM and goes for a run before a twelve-hour shift. I want my life back, I really do. I just don't know how to reach it from where I'm sitting. But no, to answer your question, no thoughts of... of not being here. Just this frustrating, heavy emptiness.
When you are sitting there for those long periods, do you find that your movements are physically slowed down, or do you feel a sense of internal restlessness that makes it hard to keep still?

Well, it's... it's definitely not restless. I'm not fidgeting or pacing or anything like that. It's more like... like I'm moving through molasses, you know? If I even move at all. I'll sit in that recliner—it's this brown leather one I've had for years, used to be the most comfortable spot in the house after a long shift—and I'll just sink into it. And if I do try to get up, say, to get a glass of water, it feels like my limbs weigh a hundred pounds each. 

I remember a few days ago, I was sitting there, and I looked at the clock on the microwave, and it was 2:15 PM. And I thought, 'I should get a glass of water.' I was thirsty. My throat was dry. But I just sat there. I looked at my hand resting on the arm of the chair, and I tried to tell it to move, to push me up, but it was like the signal from my brain just got lost somewhere along the way. It took me... I don't know, it felt like an hour, maybe it was twenty minutes, just to muster the physical energy to stand up. And when I finally did, I was moving so slow, like an old man with bad joints, just shuffling to the kitchen. 

It's not that I'm hurting, physically, it's just this incredible heaviness. Even turning my head to look out the window feels like a chore. Back when I was working, I was always moving. You have to be quick on your feet in my line of work. You get a call, you're out the door, into the cruiser, assessing the scene before you even put it in park. I was sharp. I was fast. Now, if the phone rings—and I usually just let it go to voicemail anyway—but if it rings, I'll just stare at it. I won't even reach for it. My arms just feel like lead. So, no, definitely no restlessness. Just this... this creeping, heavy slowness that makes every little movement feel like I'm trying to push a boulder up a hill.
Since this started, have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or have you lost any weight without trying?

No, I... I don't think so. I mean, my appetite isn't exactly what it used to be, but I haven't stopped eating, and I haven't lost any weight that I can tell. 

It's funny you ask that, because eating has just become... well, it's just another mechanical process now. Back when I was on patrol, you know, you're always grabbing something on the go. A sandwich here, a burger there, lots of coffee. You eat because you're burning calories and you need the energy to stay alert. You actually look forward to it, like, 'Hey, let's hit that diner on 4th street for a hot meal before the shift gets crazy.' You'd sit with your partner, talk about the calls, actually enjoy the food. But now... now I just don't care about it at all. 

But I still eat. I know I have to, logically. It's not like I'm starving myself or dropping pounds. My uniform pants, well, my regular jeans I guess, they still fit exactly the same. My belt is on the same notch it's been on for the last five years. I just... I'll manage to get up, eventually, and I'll open the fridge, and I'll just stare at whatever is in there. Usually it's just cold cuts or a frozen dinner, something that doesn't require any real effort to make, because like I said, just standing up and moving takes everything out of me. 

So I'll microwave something, usually just once a day around the evening, and I'll sit back down in that same brown leather chair and just chew it. I don't even really taste it anymore. It's honestly like chewing cardboard. There's no satisfaction in it. But I get it down. I force myself to swallow it because I know the human body needs fuel. So my weight is stable, I'm pretty sure. I haven't actually stepped on a scale in weeks, but I don't look any thinner in the mirror on the rare occasion I actually look in one. It's just that the enjoyment of a good steak or a hot slice of pizza... that's completely gone. But physically, no, no real changes in my weight or anything like that. I'm just eating to keep the engine from completely stalling out, even if it's barely idling right now.
Since this started, have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns, such as difficulty falling asleep, waking up too early, or perhaps finding yourself sleeping much more than usual?

Sleep... you know, sleep is actually the one thing that hasn't really flipped upside down on me. I haven't noticed any real changes there. 

Back when I was on active duty, doing the rotating shifts, my sleep was a complete disaster. You work a 7 PM to 7 AM shift, you come home, the sun is blazing, the neighborhood kids are out screaming, lawnmowers are going... you really have to train your body to sleep through anything. I actually installed these heavy-duty, industrial blackout curtains in my bedroom a few years ago. Best investment I ever made. They completely block out the sun, the streetlights, everything. Makes the room look like an absolute cave. 

So now, even with all this... this heaviness I was telling you about, the sitting in the recliner for hours on end... when it finally gets late enough, say around 10 or 11 at night, I'll eventually drag myself into the bedroom. And I don't really have trouble nodding off. I don't toss and turn, and I don't lay there agonizing over things or staring at the ceiling fan for hours. I think because I'm just so drained from the sheer effort of existing all day, if that makes any sense. It's a different kind of tired than physical exhaustion, but it still puts me under. I'll lay down, and I'm out pretty much as soon as my head hits the pillow.

And I don't sleep the whole day away either, which I know some people do when they get into a slump. I usually wake up right around 6 or 7 AM, just like my body is still hardwired to do from the early shifts. I don't even set an alarm anymore, my eyes just open on their own. So I'm getting my standard seven or eight hours, pretty consistently. 

The sleep itself is fine. It's just... the problem isn't the sleeping, or waking up. The problem is that once my eyes do open at 6 AM, I just lay there looking at those blackout curtains, knowing I have to pull myself out of bed and go sit in that leather chair and do nothing all over again. But the actual hours I'm asleep? No, I'm not sleeping too much, and I'm not staying awake all night. That part of my brain still seems to be punching the clock right on time.

I'm just eating to keep the engine from completely stalling out, even if it's barely idling right now.

doctor.question: Since this started, have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns, such as difficulty falling asleep, waking up too early, or perhaps finding yourself sleeping much more than usual?

patient.answer:
Sleep... you know, sleep is actually the one thing that hasn't really flipped upside down on me. I haven't noticed any real changes there. 

Back when I was on active duty, doing the rotating shifts, my sleep was a complete disaster. You work a 7 PM to 7 AM shift, you come home, the sun is blazing, the neighborhood kids are out screaming, lawnmowers are going... you really have to train your body to sleep through anything. I actually installed these heavy-duty, industrial blackout curtains in my bedroom a few years ago. Best investment I ever made. They completely block out the sun, the streetlights, everything. Makes the room look like an absolute cave. 

So now, even with all this... this heaviness I was telling you about, the sitting in the recliner for hours on end... when it finally gets late enough, say around 10 or 11 at night, I'll eventually drag myself into the bedroom. And I don't really have trouble nodding off. I don't toss and turn, and I don't lay there agonizing over things or staring at the ceiling fan for hours. I think because I'm just so drained from the sheer effort of existing all day, if that makes any sense. It's a different kind of tired than physical exhaustion, but it still puts me under. I'll lay down, and I'm out pretty much as soon as my head hits the pillow.

And I don't sleep the whole day away either, which I know some people do when they get into a slump. I usually wake up right around 6 or 7 AM, just like my body is still hardwired to do from the early shifts. I don't even set an alarm anymore, my eyes just open on their own. So I'm getting my standard seven or eight hours, pretty consistently. 

The sleep itself is fine. It's just... the problem isn't the sleeping, or waking up. The problem is that once my eyes do open at 6 AM, I just lay there looking at those blackout curtains, knowing I have to pull myself out of bed and go sit in that leather chair and do nothing all over again. But the actual hours I'm asleep? No, I'm not sleeping too much, and I'm not staying awake all night. That part of my brain still seems to be punching the clock right on time.
